title: Building Block One: The Leader's Seven Essential Behaviors
hook: Overflowing gown bins tell Hannah more about supply reality than the dashboard did.
counterintuition: Leadership may look like private character; in fact, people copy the public reaction: one calm question invites truth while one punished fact teaches silence.
tryThisNow: Walk to one place where work is done. Ask what the report is missing, then choose one priority you will inspect again this week.
keyTakeaway: Execution leadership becomes real through behaviors that keep the leader close to the work, honest about priorities, and consistent about consequences.

breakdown.fastRead:
At 7:22 a.m., Fumiko sees gowns spilling from a bin outside pre-op while the supply dashboard still says stocked. The hallway knows something the report does not.

Leader behavior is execution when it keeps you close enough to act. Know the work. Ask for the real state. Narrow the list. Check back. Praise delivery. Coach the person. Notice when pride makes truth hard to hear. These are not poster traits. They teach people which facts can reach you.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 5:55 a.m., Orla holds a cloudy milk test vial at the farm co-op meeting while three members argue that the tanker schedule is fine. Her job is not to win the argument. It is to make realism safe enough that the vote can be based on the milk in her hand.

You can see the mechanism in the first awkward pause. People tend to protect a promise after it has been spoken out loud. They smooth bad news, widen dates, and call vague ownership teamwork. Turning leadership behavior into a linked system for realism and follow-through cuts through that comfort by asking for the live fact that changes action.

At 10:09 p.m., Dinesh looks at nine launch goals on a whiteboard and knows his tired team can only carry three through Friday. The useful move is not louder pressure. It is closer contact with the work. Ask who owns the next hard move, what might block it, and what proof will be visible soon. Then stay close enough to revise the plan when the answer is rough.

At 12:03 a.m., Solange reads a correction from a junior reporter and feels her first flash of irritation before she feels gratitude. There is a limit. Strong execution cannot make a weak premise true. It can only expose the weak premise early, while a leader still has time to change the promise, move the person, narrow the goal, or stop pretending.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hannah leaves the supply dashboard open on her office monitor and walks to the pre-op hallway. The paper gown bin is overflowing. A nurse has taped a handwritten note to the cabinet because the official count says supplies are fine. The dashboard did not lie exactly. It simply knew less than the hallway.

Knowing your people and your business starts there. It is not a ceremonial walk or a leader trying to look humble. It is the discipline of getting close enough to judge reality before reports polish it. Without that contact, the other behaviors weaken. Realism becomes a slogan. Priorities become guesses. Follow-through becomes a calendar entry instead of a correction.

The seven behaviors work like a connected set. Insist on realism, and safer status language starts to lose power. Set clear goals and priorities, and people can stop pretending that every task deserves the same oxygen. Follow through, and the organization learns that a commitment is not finished when it is spoken. Reward the doers, and status moves toward the people who carry the hard middle. Coach, and capability rises without lowering the standard.

The harder behavior is self-knowledge. A leader who cannot handle embarrassment will ask for realism and then punish the first person who brings it. A leader who loves being liked will reward charm and call it morale. A leader who fears conflict will let vague ownership survive because naming it feels impolite. Emotional fortitude is not a mood. It is the ability to let the true fact stay in the room long enough to change the work.

At the orchestra rehearsal, Matthew taps measure 42 and asks the violins to start again. He does not give a speech about excellence. He names the exact entry, keeps the standard visible, and helps the section hear what has to improve. That is coaching tied to execution. The point is not kindness instead of standards or standards instead of kindness. The point is capability under a real demand.

There is a trap in treating these behaviors as a leader's private virtues. The organization does not experience your intentions. It experiences what you ask, what you inspect, what you praise, what you let pass, and what you return to after the room has moved on.

Look at one place where your reports sound cleaner than the work. Go there. Ask what the report is missing. Name one priority. Return soon enough that people learn the question mattered.

The behavior you repeat becomes the standard people trust.

These behaviors also protect one another. Direct knowledge without follow-through becomes curiosity. Realism without priorities becomes complaint. Coaching without rewards can build skill that the culture ignores. Self-awareness without action becomes private insight. The leader's job is to keep the chain connected while the work is still moving.

examples.title: Fumiko leaves the dashboard for the pre-op hallway

planSpec.domain: a hospital COO discovering a supply gap that the dashboard misses
planSpec.audience: an executive who needs to know the business by touching the work
planSpec.stakes: a surgery morning delayed by a supply truth hidden behind clean counts
planSpec.requiredBeat: she walks from dashboard certainty to the overflowing gown bin and changes the review

examples.scenario: At 7:22 a.m., Fumiko steps around a blue bin outside pre-op with paper gowns puffing over the rim like blown insulation. Her tablet says stocked, because central supply scanned the case last night. A scrub tech named Willa is tearing open the last sleeve pack with her teeth. Fumiko has a finance review in eight minutes. She is about to keep walking when Willa says, not loud, "We scan boxes, not rooms."
examples.whatToDo: Stay in the hallway, ask Willa to show the gap between scanned stock and room stock, and move that fact into the finance review.
examples.whyItMatters: Knowing the work means finding the place where the report stops seeing. Proximity lets the leader correct the measure before the delay spreads.

examples.title: Orla sets the cloudy vial beside the vote slips

planSpec.domain: a farm co-op chair forcing realism before a tanker schedule vote
planSpec.audience: a chairperson balancing member pride with a quality problem
planSpec.stakes: a failed dairy pickup and whether members can speak plainly about bad test results
planSpec.requiredBeat: she makes the vial the fact everyone must face before voting

examples.scenario: At 5:55 a.m. in the Grange hall co-op vote, "The tanker route is fine," Eamon says while Orla holds a cloudy milk test vial under the fluorescent light. "The tanker route is fine," Eamon says, arms folded over his feed-store jacket. "Then tell me what this is," Orla says, setting the vial beside the vote slips. The room smells of wet wool and coffee. She can feel the members wanting loyalty more than truth. The vote is in four minutes, and she must decide whether to let pride set the schedule.
examples.whatToDo: Put the test result in the center of the discussion, ask what it means for the route, and delay the vote until the quality fact is owned.
examples.whyItMatters: Realism is a leadership behavior because people need permission to face the fact that embarrasses the group.

examples.title: Dinesh erases six goals from the launch board

planSpec.domain: a software director narrowing launch goals during a late deploy
planSpec.audience: a leader whose team cannot execute nine priorities with one release window
planSpec.stakes: a Friday launch at risk from scattered pressure
planSpec.requiredBeat: he chooses three priorities instead of pretending nine can all carry full force

examples.scenario: The deploy console blinks amber behind Dinesh as nine launch goals fill the whiteboard. Two engineers are eating vending-machine crackers. The customer import, billing patch, and audit log all need the same reviewer before midnight. Dinesh has a marker cap between his teeth. He is about to say we need all of it when he sees the reviewer rubbing her eyes. He has to pick what the release will truly protect.
examples.whatToDo: Erase the lower-priority goals, name the three that must survive tonight, and assign follow-through checks for those three only.
examples.whyItMatters: Clear priorities turn pressure into action. Nine equal goals are not ambition, they are a refusal to choose.

examples.title: Petra notices who really carried practice

planSpec.domain: a youth soccer coach reviewing which players she rewarded after a poor tournament
planSpec.audience: a coach learning that praise can train the wrong behavior
planSpec.stakes: whether the team values delivery or visible confidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees that her praise went to talkers while quiet doers made the team function

examples.scenario: It takes Petra until 8:47 p.m. in the empty parking lot after the tournament loss to notice who really carried practice. She kept praising Ronan, the captain with the loud huddles. The drill sheets in her hand tell another story. Sibel arrived early, set every cone, paired the new players, and never once got the first shout-out. Petra writes reward the doer on the back of the lineup card before the field lights click off.
examples.whatToDo: Open the next practice by naming Sibel's concrete contributions, then tie future praise to work that improves the team's execution.
examples.whyItMatters: People copy what earns status. If visible talk gets the reward, quiet follow-through starts to look optional.

examples.title: Ilyas coaches the foreman at lathe four

planSpec.domain: a machine-shop owner coaching a foreman through a slipping queue
planSpec.audience: an owner who usually fixes the schedule himself and leaves capability unchanged
planSpec.stakes: a foreman who either learns the constraint or keeps waiting for rescue
planSpec.requiredBeat: he shifts from correcting the queue to building the foreman's skill

examples.scenario: What should Ilyas do when lathe four sits idle and the mill queue backs up? Before, he would grab the clipboard, reorder the jobs, and leave the foreman embarrassed. Today he points to the idle lathe and asks Halina what the queue is telling her. She starts with excuses, then notices the missing inspection stamp on the third job. Ilyas keeps his finger off the clipboard while she calls inspection herself.
examples.whatToDo: Coach from the constraint. Ask the foreman to read the queue, identify the blocker, and make the call while you watch.
examples.whyItMatters: Execution improves when leaders build capability, not only when they fix today's miss with their own hands.

examples.title: Solange feels the correction sting before midnight

planSpec.domain: a newsroom editor noticing her own defensiveness when a junior reporter corrects her
planSpec.audience: a leader whose emotional reaction can make honesty expensive
planSpec.stakes: whether junior staff keep surfacing errors before publication
planSpec.requiredBeat: she catches the private sting that could punish truth if she lets it drive her response

examples.scenario: You see cold tea beside Solange's keyboard while a junior reporter's correction glows in the CMS. The reporter is right. The quote attribution is wrong. Solange feels heat rise in her neck before she feels relief. Her first draft reply is clipped enough to teach a lesson nobody should learn. She deletes it, stares at the blinking cursor, and writes thank you first.
examples.whatToDo: Answer the correction with thanks, fix the line, and tell the reporter in the morning that catching errors early is valued.
examples.whyItMatters: Self-knowledge is practical. A leader's unmanaged sting can train people to hide the exact truth the work needs.

reviewCards.front: A plan sounds clear, but the next hard owner is unnamed. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the execution test: name the owner, the next action, the date, and the evidence that will prove the work moved.

reviewCards.front: A team gives calm status while field evidence feels rough. What move keeps truth close?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the raw signal from the place where the work happens, then decide what changes before the next review.

reviewCards.front: You spot a comforting story covering a weak handoff. What question breaks the spell?
reviewCards.back: Ask what must be true by a near date, who owns that proof, and what will happen if the proof does not appear.

reviewCards.front: A target was built on a false assumption. What does strong follow-through require?
reviewCards.back: Change the target, name the failed premise, and protect the system from pretending the old promise still fits reality.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: turning leadership behavior into a linked system for realism and follow-through starts with a live promise and forces it into owned action. The habit is to ask what is true now, who owns the next hard move, and what proof will appear soon.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work plan earns quick agreement, then I will ask for the owner, date, and proof point on the hardest piece before I call it ready.
If I set a health goal, then I will name the next physical setup, the time it happens, and the check I will use tomorrow.
If I keep repeating a personal promise, then I will turn it into one visible action with a time, place, and fallback.
If someone depends on me, then I will state exactly what I will do next and when they can see or hear the result.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one promise that sounds settled and write the owner, the next action, the riskiest assumption, and the proof you expect to see within seven days.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, end each serious planning conversation by asking what changed, who owns the next hard move, and what evidence will be visible before the next check-in.
